common_name: Naranja Daylily (1956 Stout Medal Dark Orange Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Naranja's evergreen crown benefits from a protective mulch in colder parts of its range.

directions: Registered by Wheeler in 1947 and awarded the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1956, Naranja carries clear, deep orange self-colored flowers up to seven inches wide that hold their color even deep into the throat, a trait that made it a benchmark orange in mid-century breeding. Scapes reach roughly three feet and open a heavy midseason flush with some extension of bloom into later summer. Foliage stays evergreen to semi-evergreen in mild climates, so gardeners in colder zones should expect more dieback over winter. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep flower counts high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Fairy Wings Daylily (1960 Stout Medal Cream-Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Fairy Wings is fully dormant, so give the crown a season to settle before expecting a full bloom flush.

directions: Registered by Lester in 1953, Fairy Wings won the President's Cup in 1957 before taking the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1960, an unusually decorated older cultivar. Its delicate cream-yellow petals carry a soft come-and-go blush of pink over a cool green throat, giving the flower a lighter, more ethereal look than the tawny daylilies common at the time of its introduction. Scapes stand about three feet tall and open an early-to-midseason flush of single blooms above dormant foliage that dies back cleanly each fall. Grow in full sun for the best bloom count and divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: May Hall Daylily (1969 Stout Medal Peach-Orchid Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; May Hall's large blooms are heavy enough that scapes appreciate some shelter from strong wind.

directions: Registered by David F. Hall in 1960 and honored with the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1969, May Hall bears unusually large, wide-petaled flowers in a delicate peach blended with orchid overtones above a pale greenish-yellow throat. Blooms can open five and a half to six inches across on three-foot scapes during the early-to-midseason flush, making it a standout among older large-flowered diploids. Foliage is dormant, dying back fully in autumn before renewing growth in spring. Site in full sun in fertile soil and divide every few years to keep clumps blooming heavily.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Ava Michelle Daylily (1970 Stout Medal Dwarf Yellow Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Ava Michelle's low, compact habit suits edging and small-space plantings.

directions: Registered by Wilmer B. Flory in 1960, Ava Michelle went on to win the American Hemerocallis Society's Stout Silver Medal in 1970, notable among medal winners for its markedly dwarf stature. Scapes rise to only about eighteen inches and carry clean light-yellow self flowers with a green throat, opening in a mid-to-late-season flush of five-inch blooms. Its semi-evergreen foliage stays low and tidy, making it useful along walkways or at the front of a mixed border where taller daylilies would overwhelm the space. Grow in full sun and divide every few years in spring as clumps thicken.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society Stout Silver Medal records

common_name: Siloam Ury Winniford Daylily (Cream Purple-Eyed Miniature)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Siloam Ury Winniford's small, patterned flowers show best planted where they can be viewed up close.

directions: Registered in 1980 by Pauline Henry of Siloam Springs, Arkansas, Siloam Ury Winniford is one of the hundreds of eyed daylilies to come out of Henry's breeding program that established the modern eyezone class. Its deep cream, ruffled petals surround a bold purple eyezone and green throat, with blooms just over three inches wide opening in an early-to-midseason flush on scapes under two and a half feet tall. Foliage is dormant and dies back cleanly each fall. Grow in full sun for the strongest eye contrast and divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Siloam Grace Stamile Daylily (Fragrant Red Miniature)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Siloam Grace Stamile's dwarf habit and fragrance make it a good candidate for edging near seating areas.

directions: Registered in 1984 by Pauline Henry, Siloam Grace Stamile is a diminutive, fragrant daylily bearing intense red flowers just over two inches across, each with a deeper red halo and a green throat. Scapes stay under a foot and a half tall, opening a heavy early-to-midseason flush of miniature blooms well suited to rock gardens and container plantings. Foliage is dormant, dying back fully in winter before regrowing in spring. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every few years as clumps become congested to keep bloom counts high.

common_name: Double Razzle Dazzle Daylily (Red Double-Form Diploid)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Double Razzle Dazzle's fully double flowers open more reliably where nights stay warm during early bloom season.

directions: Registered in 1974 by Mrs. Edgar W. (Betty) Brown III, Double Razzle Dazzle produces fully double red self flowers with a gold throat, each bloom carrying an extra ring of segments that gives it a peony-like fullness rather than the typical single daylily form. Blooms open about four inches wide on scapes just over two feet tall during the early part of the season. Foliage is evergreen, so gardeners in colder zones should expect winter dieback despite the plant's hardiness. Grow in full sun in fertile soil and divide every few years in spring to keep the double form expressing well.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lady Fingers' long, narrow petals show their twisting form best where scapes have open air movement.

directions: Registered by Peck in 1967, Lady Fingers is a long-established spider-form daylily bearing yellow-green self flowers with a green throat and an extreme petal-length-to-width ratio that later earned it the Harris Olson Spider Award in 1990. Its narrow, gracefully twisting segments open six inches long on scapes roughly three feet tall during the midseason flush, giving clumps a much airier look than round-flowered modern hybrids. Foliage is dormant, dying back fully each fall before renewing in spring. Site in full sun with room for scapes to spread and divide every few years to keep the spidery form at its best.
sources: The Spider and Unusual Form Daylily Society
